Blacktip sardinella, Sardinella melanura, is a relatively small-bodied clupeid, with field surveys indicating that the maximum total length encountered in wild populations reaches approximately 20.3 centimeters [Li = approximately 20.3 centimeters], a dimension consistent with the moderate size range observed among related sardinellas. The age at which newly spawned individuals emerge from the egg has been documented under controlled rearing conditions, showing that at a stable water temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], the incubation period lasts approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days], after which the yolk-sac larva begins its brief period of endogenous feeding. During this early developmental phase, the wet weight at birth, measured immediately following eclosion, is estimated at 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], reflecting the small pelagic egg diameter characteristic of the genus. These initial life-history parameters, including the elevated thermal optimum for development, are thought to facilitate rapid early growth in the warm, productive waters of the species' tropical Indo-Pacific range.

Growth trajectories derived from length-frequency analyses and otolith readings reveal that Sardinella melanura attains sexual maturity at a total length of approximately 12.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 12.3 centimeters], a threshold that corresponds closely to the size at which the majority of individuals in sampled populations show advanced gonadal development. The body mass associated with the onset of puberty has been calculated from length-weight regressions, yielding an estimated wet weight at puberty of 21.4 grams [Wwp = 21.4 grams], a value that aligns with the allometric scaling relationships seen in other sardines. This size at first maturation is reached relatively quickly, likely within the first year of life, allowing the species to begin contributing to the spawning stock at a young age. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this length at maturity is intermediate, reflecting a life history that balances early reproductive output against continued somatic growth toward the ultimate size limit.

The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic body mass approached by fully grown adults, has been estimated at 97.4 grams [Wwi = 97.4 grams] based on length-weight relationships derived from robust field samples. This maximum adult mass is achieved when individuals reach the ultimate total length of the species, indicating that growth in mass is strongly correlated with the attainment of skeletal size. In terms of reproductive output, females of Sardinella melanura are capable of producing approximately 70 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 70 eggs per spawning event] during the peak of the breeding season, and such intense spawning events can be sustained for approximately 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events per year] under favorable conditions, yielding a substantial annual fecundity. This high daily reproductive effort, partitioned into numerous small pelagic eggs, is a common strategy among small-bodied clupeids that experience heavy predation pressure on early life stages.

Longevity estimates for blacktip sardinella, based on mark-recapture studies and validated by the interpretation of annual growth increments on scales and otoliths, indicate that the species has a maximum lifespan of 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days] when maintained at a mean annual water temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]. Individuals reaching the upper bounds of this longevity are rare in wild catches, with most fish in exploited populations seldom exceeding five to six years of age. The interplay between a brief lifespan and early maturation at about 12.3 centimeters total length suggests that the species relies on high annual reproductive output to maintain population stability under variable environmental conditions.

Examining the reproductive biology from a seasonal perspective, the maximum reproductive rate of this species is achieved when water temperatures approach 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], a thermal regime that coincides with the peak spawning period in many tropical sardinella populations. The overall annual reproductive effort, calculated from the product of clutch size and the duration of the spawning season, underscores a strategy of high fecundity and minimal parental investment. Adult body mass plateaus at 97.4 grams [Wwi = 97.4 grams], at which point growth in length slows considerably and energetic resources are increasingly diverted toward gamete production. This trade-off between continued somatic expansion and reproductive output is a hallmark of the species' life history, and the onset of gonadal maturation at a mass of 21.4 grams [Wwp = 21.4 grams] highlights the early shift toward reproductive maturity that enables rapid population response to favorable environmental cues.
